title: Benchmark Carpentry
summary: Analyze which benchmark component captures the software and hardware execution environment necessary for reproducibility.

sections: Turning a claim into a test

blocks.md:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Analyze which benchmark component captures the software and hardware execution environment necessary for reproducibility
- Design an edge benchmark metric set that covers energy, thermal behavior, memory limits, latency, and deployed-model quality
- Evaluate why compression benchmarking requires multi-objective Pareto analysis rather than single-metric compression ratios
- Explain the function of benchmark run rules in enforcing fair and reproducible execution across submissions
- Order the stages of a controlled steady-state benchmark harness workflow from environment setup through validated statistical reporting

A claim that ResNet-50 runs faster at INT8 than at FP32 can reverse depending on whether timing starts at a JPEG on storage or at a preprocessed tensor in accelerator memory, or whether the quantized weights drop accuracy below the target floor. **Benchmark carpentry** is the craft of building a benchmark that measures what its claim says. It fixes the task, data, model, metrics, harness, system specification, and run rules so that the number the benchmark produces answers the engineering question and no other.

blocks.title: What the section covers
blocks.md:
In the book this section runs through:

- Turning a claim into a test
- Task and dataset
- Model and metrics
- Benchmark harness
- Specifications and run rules
- Interpreting results
- A complete reference benchmark

Pay attention to: Core benchmark components: problem definition, datasets, model architecture, metrics, harness, specs, run rules; Run rules and reproducibility; Compression benchmarks and multi-objective validation; Mobile/edge constraints: thermal envelopes, battery duty cycles, heterogeneous processors.

questions.q: Which core benchmark component is responsible for documenting the exact hardware model, CPU core pinning, GPU driver version, CUDA toolkit, compiler flags, and OS kernel version required to ensure experimental reproducibility?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. System specifications define the complete hardware and software environment—including CPU/GPU architectures, interconnect topology, OS version, kernel drivers, compiler flags, and library versions—necessary for third parties to replicate results. Dataset splits define training/validation partitioning; evaluation metrics define scoring mathematics; problem definitions specify the high-level task and domain objectives.
questions.hint: Think about: analyze which benchmark component captures the software and hardware execution environment necessary for reproducibility.

questions.q: When designing a benchmark suite for an edge computer vision model deployed on a battery-powered security camera with passive cooling, which set of evaluation metrics provides the most complete assessment of deployment viability?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. Edge deployment viability depends on more than speed: battery capacity, passive thermal limits, memory budget, and task quality all matter. A complete benchmark therefore needs energy, duty-cycle power, memory footprint, sustained latency after thermal stabilization, and quality on representative or critical slices. Peak offline throughput ignores thermal collapse and task quality, while file size or server-GPU accuracy alone misses the operational constraints of the deployed device.
questions.hint: Think about: design an edge benchmark metric set that covers energy, thermal behavior, memory limits, latency, and deployed-model quality.
options: Peak offline throughput in FP32 without thermal monitoring

Energy per inference (mJ), active vs. idle power consumption across the device duty cycle, memory footprint (SRAM/DRAM usage), sustained latency under thermal equilibrium, and deployed-model quality on representative and critical input slices
Only the model parameter file size on disk in megabytes
Top-1 validation accuracy measured on an uncompressed server GPU

questions.q: When evaluating model compression techniques (such as INT8 quantization or structured pruning), validating that the compressed model achieves a \$4× reduction in file size with <0.5\% top-1 accuracy loss is sufficient to guarantee proportional speedups and energy savings on any target deployment hardware.
questions.explanation: False. Model size reduction does not guarantee proportional latency speedups or energy savings on hardware. Unstructured sparsity, non-standard quantization precisions, or unsupported operator layouts can trigger CPU fallbacks, memory realignment stalls, or inefficient execution on edge NPUs that lack specialized hardware acceleration, sometimes making a compressed model slower than the dense baseline.
questions.hint: Think about: evaluate why compression benchmarking requires multi-objective Pareto analysis rather than single-metric compression ratios.

questions.q: In standardized benchmarking suites, the formal component that defines the mandatory execution constraints, convergence thresholds, warmup requirements, and statistical aggregation procedures to ensure fair cross-platform comparisons is called the ____.
questions.explanation: run rules. Run rules specify how the benchmark must be executed and reported so results remain comparable across systems. They matter because identical models or datasets can still produce incommensurable numbers if the timing window, warmup policy, or acceptance criteria differ.
questions.hint: Think about: explain the function of benchmark run rules in enforcing fair and reproducible execution across submissions.

questions.q: Order the following execution steps of a standardized benchmark harness protocol from beginning to end for a controlled steady-state measurement workflow:
questions.explanation: The correct order is: (2) Apply the selected environment controls, such as CPU affinity pinning and any documented clock policy, (4) Execute unmeasured warm-up iterations to load model weights and warm instruction/data caches, (1) Execute the timed measurement loop while collecting high-resolution hardware timestamps, (5) Perform verification check to ensure model output predictions match ground truth quality thresholds, (3) Compute summary statistics (mean, median, p90, p99, standard deviation) and confidence intervals. In this controlled steady-state workflow, environment controls are set first so the run reflects the intended operating policy. Warm-up comes before timing so initialization effects do not contaminate the steady-state claim. Output verification must complete before aggregating and reporting the final numbers for this workflow, because the statistics are only meaningful if the measured run produced valid results.
questions.hint: Think about: order the stages of a controlled steady-state benchmark harness workflow from environment setup through validated statistical reporting.
items: Apply the selected environment controls, such as CPU affinity pinning and any documented clock policy
Execute unmeasured warm-up iterations to load model weights and warm instruction/data caches
Execute the timed measurement loop while collecting high-resolution hardware timestamps
Perform verification check to ensure model output predictions match ground truth quality thresholds

questions.q: A vendor publishes a marketing claim stating their new AI accelerator achieves '\$120 TFLOP/s on Transformer inference.' Which combination of parameters is essential to make this throughput figure technically actionable and reproducible?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. Throughput depends strongly on the numerical path, batch size, sequence length, software stack, and sustained operating state. Those factors determine arithmetic intensity, kernel selection, memory traffic, and whether throttling appears. Process node and room temperature alone do not reconstruct the workload, and model size without precision or batching leaves the execution path undefined.
questions.hint: Think about: evaluate the minimum workload and execution context needed to interpret a vendor throughput claim.
options: Only the silicon process node (e.g., \$4 nm) and the data center room temperature
Numerical path (e.g., FP32 vs. FP16), batch size, sequence length, software/compiler stack version, and sustained thermal operating state
The brand of server power supply and the serial number of the host CPU
Only the parameter count of the model, without specifying batch size or precision

points: **Benchmark protocol**: The workload, software, hardware, measurement boundary, and run rules required to interpret and reproduce a result.
